Significant but small positive correlations were observed only for 2nd graders in reading at T1 and in arithmetic at T2. The remaining correlations were not statistically significant. Given the limited split-half reliability of child-level PES estimates reported in the Supplementary Material, these aggregate correlations should be interpreted cautiously.

Trial-level Effects of Local PES on PEA

In the reading task, local post-error slowing was associated with post-error accuracy, χ²(1) = 8.94, p = .003. This association differed by grade, χ²(1) = 12.71, p < .001, and varied across grade and measurement point, as indicated by a significant slowing × measurement point × grade interaction, χ²(1) = 5.14, p = .023. Simple-slope analyses showed that, for 2nd graders, greater local post-error slowing was positively associated with post-error accuracy at T1, OR = 1.08, 95% CI [1.03, 1.14], and at T2, OR = 1.15, 95% CI [1.07, 1.23]. The change in slope from T1 to T2 was not significant for 2nd graders, z = 1.39, p = .164.

For 4th graders, the association between local slowing and post-error accuracy was negative at T1, OR = 0.92, 95% CI [0.86, 0.99], but positive at T2, OR = 1.15, 95% CI [1.05, 1.25]. The change in slope from T1 to T2 was significant, z = 3.85, p < .001, indicating that the association between local slowing and post-error accuracy shifted from negative to positive among 4th graders. Thus, in reading, local slowing was adaptively associated with post-error accuracy for 2nd graders at both measurement points and for 4th graders at T2, but not for 4th graders at T1.

Post-error accuracy was higher at T2 than at T1, χ²(1) = 199.18, p < .001, and higher in 4th than in 2nd graders, χ²(1) = 79.55, p < .001. The measurement point × grade interaction was also significant, χ²(1) = 34.19, p < .001, indicating that developmental change in post-error accuracy differed between grades.

In the arithmetic task, local post-error slowing was associated with post-error accuracy, χ²(1) = 80.51, p < .001. This association differed by grade, χ²(1) = 20.30, p < .001, and the slowing × measurement point × grade interaction was significant, χ²(1) = 4.34, p = .037. Simple-slope analyses showed that greater local post-error slowing was positively associated with post-error accuracy in all grade-by-measurement-point combinations. For 2nd graders, the association was positive at T1, OR = 1.29, 95% CI [1.22, 1.36], and at T2, OR = 1.20, 95% CI [1.11, 1.29]. The change in slope from T1 to T2 was not significant for 2nd graders, z = -1.63, p = .103.

For 4th graders, local post-error slowing was also positively associated with posterror accuracy at T1, OR = 1.07, 95% CI [1.02, 1.14], and at T2, OR = 1.14, 95% CI [1.07, 1.21]. The change in slope from T1 to T2 was not significant for 4th graders, z = 1.31, p = .192. Thus, in arithmetic, local post-error slowing was consistently associated with higher post-error accuracy, although the association was strongest for 2nd graders at T1.

Post-error accuracy was higher at T2 than at T1, χ²(1) = 70.63, p < .001. The main effect of grade was not significant, χ²(1) = 2.10, p = .147, but the measurement point × grade interaction was significant, χ²(1) = 14.33, p < .001, indicating that developmental change in post-error accuracy differed between grades.

Task Performance Across Grade and Measurement Point

Because overall task performance may influence PES magnitude, we conducted supplementary mixed-effects analyses of subject-level accuracy and mean RTs. These analyses showed that performance generally improved from T1 to T2 in both tasks. In reading, accuracy increased over time, F(1, 615) = 129.92, p < .001, and RTs decreased, F(1, 615) = 211.92, p < .001. In arithmetic, accuracy also increased, F(1, 579) = 152.64, p < .001, and RTs decreased, F(1, 579) = 34.28, p < .001. These improvements were often larger in 2nd grade, as indicated by significant measurement point × grade interactions for arithmetic accuracy, F(1, 579) = 28.39, p < .001, reading accuracy, F(1, 615) = 46.14, p < .001, and reading RTs, F(1, 615) = 71.42, p < .001. Full model results and follow-up contrasts are reported in Supplementary Tables S3, S4, and S5. These findings indicate that developmental changes in PES should be interpreted in light of concurrent improvements in overall task performance.

Discussion

The present study examined children's balancing of speed and accuracy demands, specifically their post-error adjustments, in two academic domains-reading and arithmeticunder relatively strongly controlled conditions, combining a cross-sectional (comparing 2nd and 4th graders) with a short-term longitudinal design. We aimed to explore whether posterror slowing (PES) emerges reliably in curriculum-near tasks, how it develops over short periods of time in middle childhood, and whether it reflects efficient strategy use in terms of performance benefits. Overall, the findings provide strong evidence that children robustly slow down after errors in both academic domains, but they also reveal task-and age-related differences in the magnitude of PES, its developmental trajectories, and functional significance which we will discuss in detail in the following paragraphs.

Robust Presence of PES Across Tasks and Time

Consistent with our first hypothesis and in line with de Mooij et al. ( 2022), children showed clear and reliable post-error slowing in both arithmetic and reading at both measurement points. Importantly, the substantial PES was also confirmed when PES was calculated as a drift-controlled estimate, controlling for fatigues, variations in attention, and children's actual time on task (see Supplementary Material). These findings substantially extend prior work demonstrating substantial PES in children using cognitive conflict paradigms (Dubravac et al., 2022; Ger & Roebers, 2023a , 2023b; Gupta et al., 2009) to curriculum-near simple reading and arithmetic tasks administered in educational settings.

While often overlooked, elementary school children were found to detect their mistakes (substantial error monitoring; Botvinick et al., 2001; Braver, 2012; Roebers, 2017) Similar to the results reported by de Mooij and colleagues (2022), PES magnitude was larger for arithmetic than for reading (see Figure 2), at both measurement points. The somewhat larger magnitude of PES in both reading and arithmetic at the second measurement point may-at least in part -be attributable to familiarity with the task or a testretest effect. Moreover, children's speed of working through the tasks increased, making impulsive errors more likely and short reaction times of errors may have contributed to increased PES at the end of the school year. Admittedly, even small variations of item difficulty and the structure of the task can alter PES (Wessel, 2012) -which might have been more the case in our arithmetic than reading task (see also de Mooij et al., 2022). Accurate and fast word reading followed by selecting one of four alternatives may also be structurally different from arithmetic fact retrieval (with a two-choice answering format) and therefore be less a matter of trading off speed against accuracy. In other words, the difference in PES magnitude between reading and arithmetic may be due to distinct processing demands across domains. Together, we interpret the robust existence of PES in both reading and arithmetic as clear indications of children's well-developed cognitive control and monitoringbased strategic regulation competencies that vary as a function of experience, task familiarity, structural features and targeted domain.

Cross-sectional Grade Differences in PES Magnitude

In our study, there were no consistent grade differences in PES magnitude across the two academic domains. While in reading, there was only a tendency for larger PES in 4th graders, in arithmetic older children showed substantially stronger post-error adjustments at both measurement points. Thus, older children in our sample appeared -at least in some cases -more sensitive to errors than younger children and this is in line with developmental progression in metacognitive monitoring, strategy use, and the accuracy-speed trade-off (Bellon et al., 2019; Brod et al., 2020; Camerota et al., 2019; Krebs & Roebers, 2010; for a review see Roebers, 2022b). [This pattern of results was found both using the classical PES measure and the drift-controlled estimate, see Supplementary Material; Dutilh et al., 2012).]

As we assume that the underlying arithmetic and reading operations are not yet fully automated in this age, children still needed to invest substantial cognitive effort to solve the task at hand. To engage in additional cognitive control to make fine-tuned adjustments in speed, the younger children might not have enough cognitive resources remaining. Older children, in contrast, may perform successfully as they can additionally invest in PES.

Moreover, the arithmetic task was age-adjusted and thus at a comparable difficulty level for the two age groups (while the simple word reading task was easier for the older children; see Supplementary Table S3 & S4) and the finding that 4th graders in arithmetic showed larger PES is thus consistent with evidence that PES is larger under somewhat higher task demands (de Mooij et al., 2022; Ger & Roebers, 2023a , 2024; Cravet & Ger, 2026).

Longitudinal Developmental Change in PES

Our third hypothesis concerned longitudinal change in PES. The results suggest that PES increased in reading and arithmetic, independent of the PES measure used. The documented increase in PES is consistent with the notion that monitoring and strategy use rapidly advance in the early elementary school years (Schneider & Löffler, 2016) and also aligns with developmental perspectives suggesting that children learn to use error signals more effectively in this age range before PES can eventually decline with further automatization (de Mooij et al., 2022; Gupta et al., 2009). Clearly, more longitudinal data is necessary to fully understand developmental changes. Task repetition, school practice and familiarity of the tasks together with less frequent errors appeared to have affected children's PES magnitude, independent of age. Interestingly, 2nd graders' PES at the second measurement point was nearly identical to 4th graders' PES at the first measurement point, suggesting that within one school year and with the re-test occasion, 2nd graders caught up with 4th graders (see Table 1, right column). This shows that younger children can quickly learn to make fine-tuned adjustments in their strategy selection and use. Potentially, children can be trained or coached to use PES to approach speeded, multi-trial tasks in academic domains (Ger & Roebers, 2024b).

The somewhat divergence of longitudinal changes in PES between the two domains suggests that developmental changes in strategic post-error adjustments are not uniform and aligns with the adult literature (Wessel, 2012). Arithmetic fact retrieval may place greater demands on monitoring and control processes during this developmental window, whereas reading fluency in relatively proficient simple word readers-particularly in transparent orthographies or highly practiced contexts-may rely more heavily on automatized processes that are less sensitive to error detection and thus PES. Importantly, these domain-specific findings indicate that developmental changes can be detected when tasks are sufficiently sensitive, reaction time is measured at the trial level, and multiple age cohorts are included. But again, the structural differences between the reading and arithmetic tasks may also have contributed to task-specific longitudinal changes in PES. Moreover, at both measurement points, children were presented the identical items and it seems safe to assume that in the course of the school year, they have improved in both the simple word reading and the arithmetic tasks. As the performance increases also mirror, experience with the task structure itself but also general practice and schooling effects in the two domains have certainly contributed to the slight increase in PES over time. Thus, fine-tuned speed adjustments when working on academic tasks can be expected to emerge when a certain degree of competence and automatization is reached, possibly necessary prerequisites for both speeded responses and PES. This implies for educational settings, that once children have reached a certain level of competence, teachers might target the balancing of speed and accuracy in their instructions.

Functional Significance of PES (PES-PEA link)

The final goal of the study was to test whether PES reflects efficient strategy use and adaptive control by examining its association with post-error accuracy (PEA). PES used as an average slowing-down was only predictive for 2nd graders, once for reading (T1) and once for arithmetic (T2). All other links were not significant. We interpret this finding as showing that there is no general, overall, and linear effect of PES on the task's accuracy, possibly pointing to very variable strategy use. A child may once substantially slow down after an error, but the next error might remain undetected and response speed might remain unaffected, rendering the detection of a general benefit of PES at the mean level for performance accuracy unlikely. The low reliability of overall averaged PES seems to support the notion of a very variable task strategy, at least in elementary school years. Anyhow, these results have to be interpreted with caution.

In contrast, addressing local effects of PES on PEA by assessing whether PES on one trial affected PEA on this very trial, uncovered positive associations indicative of efficient strategy use. Fourth graders' shift from a negative to a positive link in reading from T1 to T2 may be due to practice effects and hint towards overcoming a utilization deficiency. The remaining links were positive already at T1 and did not substantially increase towards T2.

These overall positive results support the view of strategic and efficient speed and accuracy balancing in children's arithmetic and reading, enhancing subsequent performance (Bjorklund et al., 1997; Botvinick et al., 2001; Laming, 1968) -underlining its importance in academic contexts. The effect size was modest but reliable, aligning with prior evidence linking PES to improved performance and also confirming its age-dependency (de Mooij et al., 2022; Jacobs et al., 2024 Jacobs et al., , 2026)). Thus, PES can be considered as an often overlooked but beneficial strategy, consistent with the cognitive control view that errors trigger compensatory increases in control that help prevent error repetition. Importantly, not only were 2nd graders already able to balance speed and accuracy (see above) they seemed to rely more on slowing to improve accuracy then our 4th graders. Older children increased their response speed while maintaining or even increasing their accuracy, thus applying a somewhat different task approach.

In reading, 4th graders' negative link between local PES and PEA at the first measurement point might suggest that slowing after errors in simple word reading does not reflect an effective strategy in fluent readers. Such a pattern is consistent with the view that slowing may reflect attentional capturing by error (the error itself is processed and captures attentional resources and takes additional time; Notebaert et al., 2009). Or, because 4th graders were generally reacting much faster, these might mirror impulsive errors speaking for an inhibition account (Ridderinkhof, 2002). In fact, when reading interrupting the flow of reading after an error may be detrimental rather than beneficial for reading comprehension and thus PES might not be a productive strategy for advanced readers (see also de Mooij et al., 2022). The fact that 4th graders' negative link between PES and PEA changed into a positive link at the second measurement might mirror a different task approach due to familiarity with the specific task demands. Future studies may need to systematically vary the task demands to circumscribe under which conditions slowing down one's reading (after an error or when comprehension difficulties arise) might still be a valuable monitoring-based reading strategy.

Limitations

Several limitations of the present study should be considered. First, although the arithmetic and reading tasks were age-and curriculum-appropriate, they captured only specific and very constrained aspects of children's academic performance. Second, the study focused on two discrete grades (2nd and 4th), which may limit the precision with which developmental trajectories of PES across middle childhood can be characterized. Third, no a priori power analysis was conducted. The sample size was determined by the available longitudinal cohort rather than by prospective power considerations. Accordingly, nonsignificant effects should not be interpreted as evidence for the absence of an effect. We therefore interpret attenuated or non-significant findings cautiously and focus on the precision of the corresponding estimates, as reflected in their confidence intervals. Finally, although we accounted for grade and measurement point, individual differences in cognitive and metacognitive skills, motivation, or prior experience with speeded arithmetic and reading were not directly controlled, which may contribute to variability in PES and PEA. Future research should examine PES across a broader range of grades, tasks, and individual characteristics to more fully understand its strategic role in academic development.

Implications and Conclusions

Taken together, the present findings demonstrate that post-error slowing is a robust yet often overlooked and not well understood marker of children's implicit and strategic error-related adjustments in both reading and arithmetic. PES was found to increase over time in arithmetic and was associated with improved post-error accuracy when the local effects were considered, consistent with interpretations surrounding fine-tuned strategy use and improving micro-level cognitive control upregulations. For reading, the effects were present but somewhat small and call for further research.

The present study helps bridge the gap between laboratory-based research and educational contexts. We found clear evidence that already 2nd graders monitor their performance and strategically upregulate their cognitive control by selectively slowing down after errors to the benefit of their performance. This model predicted reaction times from post-error status (post-error vs. post-correct), measurement point (T1 vs. T2), grade (2nd vs. 4th grade), and their interactions. Because post-error status and measurement point varied within children, the models included bysubject random effects for post-error status, measurement point, and their interaction. In addition, because children were clustered within classrooms, we included a classroom-level random intercept. Grade was treated as a between-subject fixed effect and was not included as a random slope because each child belonged to only one grade. The model specification for Hypotheses 1-3 was therefore: RT ~ posterror * measurementPoint * grade + (1 + posterror * measurementPoint | subject) + (1 | classroom) To test Hypothesis 4, we examined the relation between post-error slowing and posterror accuracy at two levels of analysis. First, we tested the association at the aggregate child level. For each child, task, grade, and measurement point, we computed mean PES and mean change in PEA (post-correct accuracy -post-error accuracy in percentage) and correlated these scores separately by task, grade, and measurement point. This analysis tested whether children who showed greater average post-error slowing also showed higher average change in post-error accuracy.

The current findings provide strong support for the generality of PES in childhood and establish its presence in foundational academic skills -domains in which research on children's strategy use has neglected the balancing of speed and accuracy. From an educational point of view, more attention should be paid to children's strategy use when working under time constraints. Some children might have more difficulties balancing speed and accuracy than others and errors may in fact occur because children work too fast or miss to adapt their speed when tasks become more difficult. Coaching children concerning this accuracy-speed trade off may be productive in many ways.

treated as productive learning opportunities, not as failures. Coming back to Susie in our introductory example, Susie and her classmates might need more time for the test allowing a good balancing of speed and accuracy and fostering error monitoring and correction. Moreover, instructional practices, coaching and feedback should provide reflection prompts, motivate re-checking, and foster balancing speed and accuracy. Error handling in reading may be better addressed outside speeded contexts, for example, through feedback and guided re-reading and should be adapted to an individual's reading proficiency. Our findings also point to the possibility that educational classroom-based and timed assessment methods likely conflate domain-specific skills with monitoring and control processes, and performance might not yield the most valid and a pure picture of children's domain-specific learning progress. Given PES's theoretical and practical relevance, future work should investigate the cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms underlying these domain-specific patterns of PES, strategy use and its efficiency.
